lines.text: Empires of gold, a king richer than any in his age, and a desert city of books. This is the story of Mali, at the heart of West Africa.
By about 250 BCE, people were living at Djenne on the inland delta of the Niger, one of the oldest towns south of the Sahara.
Later, the Ghana Empire grew rich by taxing the gold and salt that crossed the Sahara on camels.
Around 1100, Timbuktu grew at the desert's edge, a trading hub that became a great centre of Islamic learning.
In the early 1200s, a prince named Sundiata Keita rose to found a new empire. His story is still sung in the Epic of Sundiata.
That empire was Mali, which came to control the gold trade of West Africa.
Its most famous ruler, Mansa Musa, made a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, carrying so much gold that prices fell along his way.
In Timbuktu, scholars and families gathered manuscripts by the hundreds of thousands, and many are kept there still.
From 1464 the Songhai Empire took over from Mali. Centred on Gao, it became the largest empire of West Africa, until Morocco broke it in 1591.
Centuries later, France conquered the land and ruled it as French Sudan.
In 1907, the Great Mosque of Djenne was rebuilt in mud brick. Each year the whole town gathers to replaster its walls.
Modibo Keita, born in 1915, would lead the country to independence and serve as its first president.
Ali Farka Toure would take the guitar of the desert to the world, the sound people called desert blues.
And Salif Keita would become known as the golden voice of Africa.
In 1960, Mali became independent from France, taking the name of its great old empire.
Assimi Goita, born in 1983, would become a colonel and lead coups in 2020 and 2021.
In 2012, rebels and jihadists seized the north, and the war that followed has shaken the country ever since.
In 2023, Mali turned away from France and joined Burkina Faso and Niger in the Alliance of Sahel States.
From the gold of Mansa Musa to the struggles of today, Mali's story runs on along the Niger.
